about: The AI pieces of the ecosystem: the Smart Graph, its MCP server, the Nuclear Developer, the Builder, how they work together and how the knowledge base is kept in step with the code.

rows.title: AI in NuclearLang: the Smart Graph, the MCP server, the Builder and your agents
rows.summary: Four pieces take a spec to tested, reviewed code: the Smart Graph (a private knowledge base on your machine), the MCP server `nuclear-mcp`, the Builder (the pipeline) and Nuclear Chat. The work is done by the agents and API providers you choose; NuclearLang's local agents (the Nuclear Developer) are on standby (ADR-platform-0013).
body: | Piece | What it is | Where it runs |
| Nuclear Smart Graph | the knowledge base of the whole ecosystem, searched instead of guessing | `127.0.0.1:7878` |
| The MCP server (`nuclear-mcp`) | gives any agent the graph, the compiler, a project's commands and the generators | started by the AI client, over stdio |

| Nuclear Developer (on standby) | the local agents: coder, tester, security reviewer, planner, analyst, documenter, diagnoser, acceptor, assistant; not installed nor started while the local models are on standby | `127.0.0.1:7879` |
| The Builder | the pipeline from a spec to deployed code: specification, generate, plan, tests first, code, verification, security, artifacts, deploy | the editor, or `nuclear-builder` |

| Nuclear Chat | the factory's workplace: channels, direct messages and threads with the members of your teams, who answer through their providers (a team's tech lead for the team) | `127.0.0.1:7880`, a token from the keyring |

The idea: what a model needs about Nuclear comes from the graph, and what it writes is checked by the compiler. Standard code is written by generators, not by a model. The agent or provider you choose (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, an API model) writes the rest, validates and corrects only what is wrong.

On your machine run the Smart Graph (with its own model) and Nuclear Chat, on `127.0.0.1`. Your code goes out only to the agent or provider you chose, and when you import a spec from Jira or GitHub, read an API's answer or documentation, or deploy.

Set up once: `nuclear-builder setup --profile remote --yes` (the installer's last step, with no question; VS Code has it as a wizard). It installs the Smart Graph, the MCP server and Nuclear Chat and starts them at every login; an update takes away what an earlier version installed for the local models.

rows.title: The Nuclear Smart Graph: the knowledge base of the ecosystem
rows.summary: The Smart Graph is the local, private library of everything NuclearLang is: typed cards on shelves (concepts, language, platforms, tools, errors, capabilities, playbooks, examples, docs), linked to each other, searched by meaning and by exact name, with the exact facts of the ecosystem in a relational database for the questions that have one right answer. Agents ask it instead of guessing.
body: - **Shelves.** Each shelf answers one kind of question: *concepts* (what, why, how), *language* (how it is written), *platforms* (kinds, decorators, layout), *tools* (every command, MCP tool, route, generator, agent), *errors* (what went wrong and its fix), *capabilities* (what can and cannot be done), *playbooks* (how a task is done, step by step), *examples* (validated code) and *docs* (the long documents).

- **Cards.** A row is one card with a stable id (`error:N0114`, `kind:backend.usecase`, `tool:nuclear.gen.resource`), a title, a summary, a body and links to other cards. A card can be fetched by its id, with no search.
- **A graph.** Cards link to each other with typed edges: an error to the errors it comes with and to its fix, a kind to its decorators, a playbook to the tools of its steps.

- **Hybrid search.** A query is matched by meaning (a local embeddings model) and by the exact names it writes (`N0114`, `gen resource`, `usecase`), and a card is also found by the questions it answers. The search is exact: every card a filter matches is compared with the question, so a card the graph holds is always found.

- **Exact answers.** A question that asks which, how many or what are (every tool of the MCP server, the parameters of a tool, the commands that create a kind, what a diagnostic means, the stages of the Builder) is not answered by meaning: the graph keeps the names and structured fields of every card in a relational database (SQLite, in memory only, made from the sealed cards) and a catalogue of exact questions (the `queries` shelf), each with the query that answers it. A planner matches the question to the catalogue and to the shelves: the query runs only when its exact question is closer to what was asked than the closest card, so "what is nuclear" gets its card and not the commands of the tool of that name. It fills the query's parameters from the question's own words and runs it, with no model: the answer is every row, the same every time. Nuclear Atlas shows those rows as they are, under the agent's explanation.
- **Two readers.** A local agent reads only Nuclear (`agents`); a frontier model also reads the dialects underneath, the decisions and the state.
- **Private.** It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, refuses web pages, gives nothing without a token the user allowed, and stores its texts encrypted.
- **Versioned.** The base has a schema and a revision; a check fails when it is behind the code.

Use it: `nuclear-graph search "<question>"`, `nuclear-graph answer "<question>"` (the exact rows, then the cards), `nuclear-graph card <id>`, `nuclear-graph stats`; from an AI client, the MCP tools `graph_search`, `graph_answer` and `graph_card`. The graph itself is written in Nuclear (the `python` dialect).

rows.title: The MCP of NuclearLang: what it is and how it works
rows.summary: MCP is the Model Context Protocol: the open protocol through which an AI client (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI) starts a program and calls its tools. `nuclear-mcp` is that program for NuclearLang: it gives the client the generators, the Smart Graph, the compiler, the `nuclear` commands and the internet as tools.
body: **How it works.** The AI client starts `nuclear-mcp` and talks to it over stdio. The server offers tools and a set of instructions; the instructions send a model that knows nothing about Nuclear to `nuclear_start` first (what Nuclear is, the rules, the work cycle on this machine, the atlas of every topic, each read with `nuclear_doc`). The model calls a tool, the server runs it on your machine (a search in the graph, `nuclear check`, `nuclear gen`) and answers text the model reads.
**Connect it.**
```sh
nuclear-builder setup                                # once: the AI services, and MCP clients' access to the graph
claude mcp add --scope user nuclear -- nuclear-mcp   # Claude Code
codex mcp add nuclear -- nuclear-mcp                 # Codex

Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`) and OpenCode (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`): an MCP server whose command is `nuclear-mcp`. VS Code's *Settings and integrations* (`Ctrl+Alt+S`) adds it with a button.
**Its tools, by group.**
- Learning Nuclear: `nuclear_start` (the first call), `nuclear_doc` (one topic of the atlas).

- Workspaces, specs and teams (spec 022), each change asked first: `workspace_create`, `workspace_show`, `workspace_edit`, `workspace_delete`, `app_add`, `app_rename`, `app_remove`; `spec_create`, `spec_list`, `spec_show`, `spec_edit` (written where Nuclear Builder reads them); `team_list`, `team_show`, `team_create`, `team_edit`, `team_delete`, `member_add`, `member_edit`, `member_remove`, `skills_set`. The server asks the user through the client (MCP elicitation); a client that cannot ask gets a preview and a `confirm` token (one use, 5 minutes, bound to that exact change) to call again with, after the user's yes.

- A project's tests: `project_test(project)` builds it and runs them, with the same answer in every dialect (`passed`, `failed`, each failure at its `.nuc` line). The database of a backend project, each change asked first: `project_migrate(project, action)` with `status`, `make` (`message`), `up` and `down` (`to`: a migration; `fake`: only the history; `transaction`: all, each or none; `rename` with `make`: the tables and columns that were renamed, `<table>=<new table>` or `<table>.<column>=<new column>`); the same in every backend dialect.

- Nuclear Builder, as the editor does it (0.87), each change asked first: the specs moved, migrated, deleted, a draft accepted or discarded (`spec_move`, `spec_migrate`, `spec_delete`, `spec_accept`, `spec_discard`); the runs (`run_start`, `runs`, `run_file`, `run_journal`, `run_answer`, `run_resume`, `run_retry`, `run_restart`, `run_stop`; a paid run's spending is confirmed in the editor only); QA's checks (`checks`, `check_switch`, `check_add`, `check_mark`); the teams' extras (`team_duplicate`, `team_default`, `team_export`, `team_import`, `team_logo`, `team_suggest`, `team_name_suggest`, `team_runnable`, `team_roster`, `team_temperaments`); the whole member card through `member_edit`; the skills library (`skills_*`); the line, the CI file, the connections, the reports, the agents and models (`line_show`, `line_set`, `ci_export`, `connections_check`, `metrics`, `agents_list`, `models_list`).

- What the editor does and the server does not (start or debug a run of an app, a device, HTTP Connections, the chat's channels, the vault, the settings) is listed screen by screen in `nuclear_doc("mcp")`, section 4, with where the user does it: a model says so instead of pretending.
- The generators: `project_inspect`, `generate_component`, `generate_resource`, `generate_usecase`, `generate_screen`, `api_inspect`.

- The graph: `graph_strategy` (which kind of request it is and the plan of that kind: the first call after `nuclear_start`), `graph_answer`, `graph_search`, `graph_card`, `graph_prompt`, `graph_remember`, `graph_monitor` (the hot spots of the last run with `--monitor`, kept for later).

- The compiler and the command line: `project_monitor` (where the app is slow: the report of `nuclear run --monitor`), `nuclear_check`, `nuclear_build`, `nuclear_fmt`, `nuclear_help`, `nuclear_brief`, `nuclear_defs`, `nuclear_project` (new, build, install, test, check, analyze, make, gen, migrate, add, remove, explain).
- The internet: `web_search`, `web_read`.
**The way of working it asks for.** The generators write the standard code; the model writes the rest, validates (`nuclear_check`, `nuclear test`) and corrects only what is wrong.
Each tool has its row: `mcp:generate_resource`, `mcp:graph_search`... and the whole server is `mcp:server`.
The local developer is on standby (ADR-platform-0013, `limit:remote-agents-only`): the server registers no `developer_*` tool on any machine, and tells the model to write what the generators do not.
- `project_monitor` returns what the app is doing: its state, the console of its last run (requests, errors) and, when measured, the hot spots (can:watch-the-app).

rows.title: The Nuclear Developer: the local AI agents (on standby)
rows.summary: The Nuclear Developer, a team of local agents on models of at most 3B parameters (on Ollama), is on standby (ADR-platform-0013): no set-up installs it, no MCP tool, team or chat uses it, and an update takes it away. The AI work is done by the agents and API providers you choose. Its code stays in the tree, behind the switch `localModels` of Nuclear Builder's `setup.json`.
body: **What to use instead.** An agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build) with the MCP server `nuclear-mcp`, or an API provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter) as a member of a Nuclear Builder team; Nuclear Atlas and the chat answer with the first agent installed (`faq:local-models`).
**What it was**, kept for the day the switch is turned on again (a decision of the user):

It is the junior developer of a frontier model: it writes one small piece well when the task is precise, and it does not make architecture decisions. It is itself a Synapsis backend written in Nuclear.
**Why it works with a small model.**
- A small model follows fixed steps better than it chooses tools, so each agent is a graph of fixed steps.
- What the model cannot remember comes from the Smart Graph: the card of the kind it writes, validated examples, the mistakes to avoid.
- What it writes is checked by the compiler before it answers; an error goes back to it with its card, at most three times.
- Standard code is not written by the model at all: the generators write it.
- It reads the project by itself: the files that declare the names its order writes are its context.
- Its answer is held to the order's own words: a name, a call or a value the order writes and the answer lacks is asked for once more.
- It reads and writes only Nuclear, never the target language.

**The agents** (each has its row: `agent:coder`, `agent:tester`...): the coder writes one `.nuc` file; the tester writes the tests; the security reviewer reports findings; the planner splits a spec into pieces of one file; the analyst says which kind of request a spec is; the documenter writes what a run did; the diagnoser says why a step failed and what to do; the acceptor holds each acceptance criterion against what a run left; the assistant answered Nuclear Atlas, the editor's chat.
**Roles.** Developer is one of its faces. It also works as tester, security reviewer, planner, documenter and support (`role:developer`, `role:tester`, `role:security`, `role:devops`...).

**It knows its limits.** One file per call, an 8192-token window by default, no decisions. Its plan says what of a spec the platform cannot do yet or is beyond a local model; a task beyond it is split smaller, handed to a frontier model that leads, or asked back to the user (`limit:agent-reasoning`, `playbook:escalate`).

With the switch on it ran as `nuclear-developer` (on `127.0.0.1:7879`); its models: `qwen2.5-coder:3b` writes code, `gemma4:e2b` plans and reviews, and the chat answers with its own small one (`CHAT_MODEL`, `qwen3.5:2b`).

rows.title: The set-up of the AI services: the profile `remote`
rows.summary: One set-up installs the Smart Graph, the MCP server and Nuclear Chat: `nuclear-builder setup --profile remote --yes`, the installer's last step (no question), a wizard in VS Code. It has one profile, `remote`: no local model, no Ollama; `lite`, `medium` and `hard` are on standby (ADR-platform-0013) and refused. It starts the graph and Nuclear Chat at every login.
body: | Profile | Models | Downloads | Memory | Runs on this machine |
| `remote` | none (the Smart Graph's own) | 0.3 GB | 2 GB | the Smart Graph and Nuclear Chat |

The Smart Graph's model is EmbeddingGemma in ONNX (0.3 GB), run inside the graph's own process: no Ollama. The AI work is done by the agents and API providers you choose (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build; Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter).

**On standby.** The profiles `lite`, `medium` and `hard` (Ollama, the Nuclear Developer, the local chat model) stay in Nuclear Builder's data and code but are not offered: `nuclear-builder setup --profile lite` exits with code 2 and says they are on standby; an installer given one takes `remote` and says so. Turning them on again is a decision of the user (`localModels` in Nuclear Builder's `setup.json`).

**An earlier local profile.** The set-up's first step, *Take away the local models NuclearLang no longer uses*, removes the Developer's service and launcher, the models NuclearLang pulled and Ollama when NuclearLang installed it (what was there before stays), writes `ai.env` as `remote` and says the GB freed.

**What the set-up needs**: NuclearLang with its AI archive (a Python of its own with the services and the set-up, written in Nuclear: no Python, uv or Node.js on the machine). From the source tree it also needs `uv`.

**Where things are.** The choice: `~/.config/nuclearlang/ai.env` (`%APPDATA%\nuclearlang\ai.env`): the mode, the profile, the ports. The code of the services: `~/.local/share/nuclearlang/ai/`. The graph's data and its model: `~/.local/share/nuclear-graph/`.

**The services at login.** Linux: the systemd user units `nuclear-graph` and `nuclear-chat` (`systemctl --user status|restart ...`, `journalctl --user -u nuclear-graph`). macOS: two launch agents (`io.github.nuclearlang.graph`, `.chat`). Windows: a script of the Startup folder. In idle both take about 150 MB of memory.

**Update and remove.** `nuclear update`, or the installer again, sets the services up again with `remote`, without questions. `nuclear-builder setup --remove` takes the services away and the MCP server out of each client; the graph's data stays (`--remove --all`, and the installer's `--uninstall`: everything it made, with the models and Ollama an earlier version installed).

**The ports.** `127.0.0.1:7878` the graph, `7880` Nuclear Chat; a port another program holds is replaced by the next free one, written to `ai.env` (`NUCLEAR_GRAPH_PORT`, `NUCLEAR_CHAT_PORT`). Nuclear Chat's token is made the first time and kept only in the keyring; a host reads it with `nuclear-chat connect --json`.

rows.title: The Nuclear Builder: the software factory from a spec to a pull request
rows.summary: The Builder takes a spec through six stations on your machine (Analysis, Design, Tests first, Code, Quality, Delivery), each worked by a role of the run's team: a provider's agent or a provider's model. It stops at its gates for you, documents every station in the spec's folder (`specs/<component>[/<layer>]/<id>/`), and any station or step can run again.
body: 1. **Analysis** (Analyst): the spec read as the client's request, the acceptance criteria made checkable, the questions to answer first; the analysis decides the strategy and the stations that run (`concept:strategies`). `analysis.md`, `questions.md`.

2. **Design** (Architect): the generators write first what follows from the data (`nuclear gen resource`); then the design, its Mermaid diagrams and ADRs, and a plan of one-file pieces. `design.md`, `plan.md`.
3. **Tests first** (Developer): the tests from the acceptance criteria and the plan, before any code. `test-plan.md`.

4. **Code** (Developer): what the generators did not write; each use case wired by `nuclear gen usecase`; repaired with the compiler (`nuclear fix`, then `nuclear check` errors to the agent); the lead takes what is left.

5. **Quality** (QA): its plan goes into the run's checks and stops for you (switch checks, add your own, run yours); then the build and the tests, up to three repair rounds told by `nuclear explain`, the acceptance criteria held against the result. `qa-report.md`.

6. **Delivery** (DevOps): the definition of done, the user stories and the pull request's text, and the infrastructure the change needs (the CI exported from the line, the deployments and environments, the containers, the monitoring, the secrets); once you approve, the branch, the commit in your name and the pull request with `gh`, never merged.

- **Big work only, and several specs in one run** (spec 024): a small or medium task is the agent's (`playbook:size-a-task`); a run takes one spec or several, each through every station before the next, one bill. A station that fails is diagnosed once by its role's provider and, when the diagnosis says it can be fixed, works once more with it, within the budget (a failed Quality is repaired by the Code station, then judged again); what a station cannot fix alone is asked of you with its diagnosis (your decision works it once more), and what only you can decide (your CI host, a repository) is listed at its gate; a check fixes what it finds in its station's documents and fails only for what it could not fix. Every step, approval, failure and repair is told in the team's channel with its log folded, and the run's diagram reads first as five business steps for a product owner (Understand, Design, Build, Check, Deliver), the tool calls behind *technical details*.

- **The team** is the members the user hires, any number per role, each worked by a provider's agent or an API model (the local kind is on standby, ADR-platform-0013: a member of it is converted on read) (`nuclear-builder team …`, the new-team wizard in VS Code; no presets, ADR-platform-0010); a station is worked by the member the tech lead assigned, else the role's first. One budget per run (5 USD by default); anything paid is confirmed twice unless the user turned that off, and `forceConfirm` brings the questions back.
- **Where**: VS Code (`Ctrl+Alt+P`), Android Studio (`Alt+Shift+P`), a terminal (`nuclear-builder run specs/<component>/<id>/spec.md`), or `/task <text>` in Nuclear Atlas.
- **The gates**: after Analysis, Design and before Delivery by default (`.nuclear/builder.json` `gates`); `nuclear-builder run --resume <id>` goes on.
- **The journal**: `.nuclear/builder/runs/<id>.md`, next to the run file `<id>.json` the editors draw.

- **When it fails**: the diagnoser says why; `nuclear-builder retry <id>` goes on from the step that failed, keeping every step before it (the Developer's code too); `--from <station>` runs a station again and `--step <step>` one step with every step after it; `nuclear-builder restart <id>` runs it all again. A retry or a restart that would take files back asks first (refused without `--yes` outside a terminal; the page and the tools ask the user), and every file the engine takes back is set aside first in `.nuclear/builder/runs/<id>.set-aside/`: no agent's work is lost.
- **On a server**: `nuclear-builder ci` runs the commands of `.nuclear/builder.json` and `nuclear-builder export github|gitlab|bitbucket` writes the CI file.

- **Retries, smallest first** (2026-11-23): a call or command that fails is tried again in place (2 times), then its part of the station (once), then the station's repair (once), then the run waits for the user (Retry / End as failed / Later): it never ends failed by itself while something can be retried. A failure never takes the agents' files out of the project. What is not worth retrying (budget, a missing key or model, 401/403) goes to the user at once. The bounds: `.nuclear/builder.json` `retries`.

rows.title: Generators first: the tools write the standard code, the agent you choose writes the rest
rows.summary: The order of work is fixed: the generators write the standard code, and the agent or API provider you choose (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build; an API model) writes what is left, validates with the compiler and the tests, and corrects only what failed. The local developer that wrote small pieces under a lead is on standby (ADR-platform-0013).
body: 1. **Understand the whole** (the spec, the project, the architecture): `nuclear_start`, `project_inspect`, `graph_strategy`.
2. **The tools write what is standard**: `generate_resource` for every resource the spec names; `generate_usecase` wires each use case (its alias in the facade, its route).
3. **The agent writes the rest**, one small piece at a time: the path, the kind, the names it must use and the files it depends on (`nuclear_brief` and `graph_search` before writing `.nuc`).
4. **Validate**: `nuclear_check` of the project and `nuclear test`.
5. **Correct only what is wrong**, never what passed.
In the Builder the same order runs as stations, each worked by a team member: an agent or an API model (`concept:loop`).

Why this order: the cheapest worker that can do a step does it. A generator costs nothing and never fails; a model costs tokens, so it is used for what only it can do: understanding, judgment and the code no generator writes.

rows.title: How the knowledge base stays in step with the code: assets, revisions and the check
rows.summary: The knowledge base is asset files in `nuclear-graph-storage/data`: most rows are generated from the working tree, the rest are written by hand and name their sources. It has a schema and a revision; `nuclear-graph knowledge check` fails when a row is behind the code, and every finished feature ends with build, check and ingest.
body: - **Generated rows** are read from a structured source and never edited: the compiler's diagnostics, the standard library, each platform's kinds, decorators and layout, the help of the four CLIs, the MCP tools, the HTTP routes, the Builder's stages, the agents, the editor's commands, each component's version, the example projects and every document section. They cannot drift: building again rewrites them.

- **Curated rows** are written by hand (the purpose, the concepts, the playbooks, the capabilities, the failures). Each names the `sources` it was written from. When a source changes, the check asks for a review of that row.
- **Overlays** add hand-written fields (links, examples, questions) to generated rows.

- **Versions.** `manifest.json` holds the schema (the row format), the revision (it rises by one whenever any row changes) and, per row, its hash and the revision that last changed it. `revisions.json` is the log. The graph remembers the revision it ingested.
The commands:
```sh
nuclear-graph knowledge build     # write the generated assets, validate everything, raise the revision
nuclear-graph knowledge check     # fail when the assets, a curated row or the graph are behind the tree
nuclear-graph knowledge review    # record that a curated row still holds after its source changed
nuclear-graph ingest              # the graph learns the new revision (only what changed is embedded)
A build refuses an invalid base: a link to a row that does not exist, a duplicated id, or target-language code in a row the local agents read.
The rule for whoever changes the ecosystem (a person or an agent): a feature is not done until `knowledge check` is clean and the graph holds the new revision.

rows.title: Strategies: how the agent decides what to do with a request
rows.summary: Each kind of request a user makes has a strategy: a row that says how the kind is recognised, its plan with the tool of every step and what it asks of a run. No model chooses it: the request's exact signs decide, then its meaning. 31 kinds, from a whole system to a failing test.
body: A whole system, one screen, a rename and a failing test are not done the same way. So before anything is generated or planned, the **analyst** says which kind of request it is, and the run follows the strategy of that kind (ADR-developer-0001).
| Family | Strategies |

| create | `strategy:system`, `strategy:project`, `strategy:component`, `strategy:resource-api`, `strategy:resource-db`, `strategy:client-of-backend`, `strategy:interface`, `strategy:repository`, `strategy:usecase`, `strategy:endpoint`, `strategy:declaration` |
| change | `strategy:member`, `strategy:refactor-rename`, `strategy:refactor-move-extract`, `strategy:refactor-architecture`, `strategy:data-migration`, `strategy:configuration`, `strategy:remove` |
| fix | `strategy:bug-compile`, `strategy:bug-failing-test`, `strategy:bug-behaviour`, `strategy:bug-runtime`, `strategy:bug-data-contract`, `strategy:bug-interface`, `strategy:bug-environment` |
| verify and explain | `strategy:tests`, `strategy:security-review`, `strategy:document`, `strategy:question`, `strategy:operate` |
| beyond | `strategy:beyond` |

**How a kind is recognised.** By the request's exact signs first (a diagnostic code, a test's output, `rename A to B`, a `GET <url>` line, a `VERB /path` line), then by its words and its meaning, and by whether the project already has the names it writes. The answer says which signs chose it.

**What a strategy decides.** The stages of the Builder that run (a compile error needs no Generate, a rename no tests first); where the pieces come from (the planner, the files that declare what changes, or a tool that already rewrote them); the generators it calls; the facts it cannot start without, asked to the user instead of guessed; whether it needs a frontier model to lead.

**Tools before models.** In every strategy a generator writes what is standard, the compiler's exact fixes come before any repair, a rename is done by a tool, and a model writes only a piece of one file that no tool can write.
**Ask it.** `nuclear-graph strategy "<request>"` in a terminal; `graph_strategy` over MCP; the Analysis step of a Builder run. A spec may name its strategy itself: `- Strategy: usecase`.

rows.title: The software factory: stations, roles as files, providers as assignments, teams
rows.summary: Every spec goes through six stations, each owned by a role: Analysis (Analyst), Design (Architect), Tests first and Code (Developer), Quality (QA), Delivery (DevOps: the infrastructure and the delivery; its id `delivery` of before is read as `devops`). A role is a folder of files, nuclear-agents/roles/<role>/, that every provider reads; who does a role is the user's choice.
body: Spec 011 and ADR-platform-0005 make Nuclear Builder a **software factory**: the same stations, in the same order, for every spec.
| Station | Role | What it delivers (in `specs/<id>/`) |
| Analysis | Analyst | `analysis.md` (the acceptance criteria made checkable), `questions.md` |
| Design | Architect | `design.md` (components, diagrams, the ADRs it follows), proposed ADRs, `plan.md` |
| Tests first, Code | Developer | the tests (TDD), then the code; `work-log.md` |
| Quality | QA | `test-plan.md` first, for the user to approve; then `qa-report.md` (functional and non-functional checks, edge cases, security, good practices, load and performance) |

| Delivery | DevOps | `definition-of-done.md`, `user-stories.md`, the project's documents, `pr.md`, `deployment.md` when the change touches the CI, the deployments, the containers, the monitoring or the secrets; pushes only when the user approves and never merges |

**A role is a folder** (`nuclear-agents/roles/<role>/`, ADR-developer-0002): `role.md` (mission, inputs, outputs, definition of done, what it never does), `skills/*.md`, `templates/*.md`, `checks.toml` (each check on or off, at a station, run by the role or by the user), and `roster/{en,es}.json` (the 40 satirical employees the user hires for it, each with a temperament of `roles/temperaments.json`: extrovert, shy, nerd…) with their painted cyberpunk portraits in `roster/faces/<id>.webp`, made by a local image model (FLUX.1-schnell through stable-diffusion.cpp) that `roles/faces.nuc` drives from each employee's profile, temperament and gender (ADR-developer-0003).

**The prompts of the local agents are the roles' skills**: a skill whose front matter names a prompt (`prompt: agent.repair`) is ingested into the graph's `prompts` collection, so `graph_prompt` and the Nuclear Developer (on standby) read the same text. A change to one is a new evaluation round.

**Who does a role** is an assignment: a provider's agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build) or a provider's model through an API (the local agents are on standby, ADR-platform-0013), chosen per member of a **team**. A team (ADR-platform-0010) is the members the user hires from the rosters, any number per role (twenty developers if so), one of them the tech lead; it is made with a five-step wizard (identity with a suggested name, purpose and skills, members suggested from them, the roster with filters, who works each member with every paid one marked), never from a preset. A station is worked by the member the tech lead assigned for the run (`run --assign`), else the role's first member; one budget per run, confirmed twice before any money is spent.

**Skills are real files** (spec 011 requirement 34): the library `nuclear-agents/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` (Claude Code's format; domains such as payments, bank accounts, authentication, offline sync; technologies such as the Synapsis backend, mobile and web, WebSockets, SQL, Ollama, CI; practices such as TDD, an OWASP review, clean architecture) and `nuclear-agents/agents/<id>/agent.md` (backend, mobile and web engineers, a QA security tester, a tech writer). A team attaches library skills (`skills`) every member inherits and keeps its own (`ownSkills`, cloned or written in the skills editor); a member has the same and a base `agent`. A member's own skill wins over the team's, the team's over the library's. Commands and MCP tools: `nuclear-builder skills list|show|clone|create|update|delete`, `team skills set` (deleting one of the user's asks the user). Every provider gets them whole: Claude Code as plugin skills, OpenCode, Codex and Gemini CLI in their agent files, an API model in its prompt.

A team also has its model for every member (a member's own wins), its method (Scrum by default) and its instructions, which the tech lead and every member follow; why a team costs no more tokens and how its tech lead plans: concept:why-a-team.

rows.title: Why work with a team: a tech lead, stations and checks, like a human development team
rows.summary: A team does not cost more tokens than one agent doing the same work: it spends them in order. Its tech lead plans and explains before acting (what, how, who), each part goes through stations with a check between them (analysis, design, tests first, code, quality, delivery), and the team follows the method and instructions its user wrote (Scrum by default). Atlas only informs and sends tasks to a tech lead.
body: **What a team is.** The people of a human development team, played by the agents and API providers you choose: a tech lead and members by role (Analyst, Architect, Developer, QA, DevOps). One model can work the whole team (the team's model), and any member may have its own.

**Why it does not cost more.** The tokens go into the same work an agent alone would do; a team only puts them in order. Each station gets the context it needs (the spec, the design, the tests), not the whole conversation, so prompts stay short; a check between stations stops a wrong step before the next one builds on it, so less work is thrown away and done again. What costs money is said: the spending question is asked only for work paid by use (an API key); an agent's subscription is not asked.
**How it works.**

1. You ask a tech lead in Nuclear Chat, in its direct message, its team's channel, or the channel of the workspace or project its team is assigned to (Atlas tells you which team is free, or helps you make one). Each channel keeps its own memory of what was asked and done there, so a team's channel is the context of that team's work.
2. The tech lead answers first with the plan: what it will do, through which stations, and who of its team does each part.

3. It writes the spec with its acceptance criteria and starts the run in Nuclear Builder; each station is done by its member and checked (the tests first, then the code that passes them, then quality).
4. Progress is told in the thread; the gates that need you (a delivery, a destructive step, money) wait for you.

**Your rules.** Each team has a method (Scrum by default: a backlog of specs, a sprint of runs, a review at the end, or the method you write) and instructions (your conventions, what to avoid, how to report); the tech lead and every member follow them.

**Atlas and the tech leads.** Atlas explains Nuclear and your projects from the knowledge base; it does not do tasks. The chat lists Atlas and each team's tech lead; the other members work through the runs.
Set it up: *Your software company* (the teams page) — the team's model, method and instructions; by chat, the MCP server's team tools (each change asked first).
